title: Virtual Machines (Advanced)
reading:
Today's menu

By the end of this lunch you will be able to:

- Compare a single VM, an availability set and availability zones by what they survive and the SLA each one earns.
- Choose between Flexible and Uniform orchestration for a Virtual Machine Scale Set, and plan explicit outbound access.
- Design an autoscale setting with metric rules, schedule profiles and cool-downs that won't flap.
- Explain how images, cloud-init, extensions, upgrade policies and automatic repairs keep many instances identical and healthy.
- Decide when Spot VMs, dedicated hosts and proximity placement groups fit, and how Azure Update Manager and Trusted Launch keep a fleet patched and secure.

Meanwhile at Nusantara Retail

Every year on 12 December — Harbolnas, Indonesia's national online shopping day — traffic to the storefront jumps for a few hours. Last year the old pantry server froze seven minutes after midnight, and the flash sale ended before it started. This year the shop already runs in Azure, but on two fixed-size VMs behind a load balancer.

Ibu Sari has two rules. "I will not pay for ten servers all year for one night. And I don't want anyone awake at midnight clicking buttons." Dewi asks how ten servers would stay identical and patched. Pak Budi reminds everyone that a whole datacenter can fail. And the finance team has read about cheap "spare" Azure capacity and wants to know whether the shop can use it.

So today's question: how does the storefront grow for the 12.12 peak, survive the loss of a datacenter, and shrink again by breakfast — on its own?

Reading

1. Availability: what can fail, and what each option survives

Start with the failures you are designing for. A single host can fail or be rebooted for maintenance. A rack can lose its power supply or network switch. A whole datacenter — an availability zone — can lose power, cooling or networking. A region can fail too, but that is disaster recovery (Lunch 17). Each VM availability option protects against a different slice of that list.

A single VM relies on Azure to restart it on a healthy host after a hardware fault, and its SLA depends on its disks (Lunch 06). An availability set groups two or more VMs in one datacenter and spreads them across up to three fault domains — groups of servers that share a power source and network switch — and up to 20 update domains, groups that Azure reboots together during planned maintenance, one at a time, with 30 minutes for each to recover before the next. Availability sets cost nothing extra and keep VMs physically close, but they cannot survive the loss of the datacenter itself. Availability zones put VMs in physically separate datacenters within the region, so a zone outage removes only part of your capacity. A VM is either zonal — pinned to the zone you choose — or regional, placed wherever Azure finds room, with no zone promise at all. A zone-spanning scale set does the pinning for you and keeps the zones balanced.

Azure helps even a lone VM more than people expect. When a host fails, service healing restarts the VM on a healthy host automatically. Most planned platform maintenance either doesn't touch running VMs or pauses them for a few seconds, and when a reboot or pause is coming, the Scheduled Events endpoint inside the VM announces it so a well-written application can drain its connections first. None of that removes the downtime of a restart, though — only a second VM somewhere else does.

Option | Survives | VM connectivity SLA (October 2026) | Good to know
Single VM, all disks Premium SSD or Ultra Disk | Host failure, after an automatic restart | 99.9% | Standard SSD: 99.5%; Standard HDD: 95%
Availability set, 2+ VMs | Host and rack failures, planned maintenance | 99.95% | One datacenter; fault and update domains fixed at creation
2+ VMs across 2+ availability zones | Host, rack and whole-datacenter failures | 99.99% | Zone-redundant load balancer frontends and disks help

These figures come from the Microsoft service level agreements at the time of writing; check them before you promise anything to a director. Remember what they cover: connectivity to a VM, not your application. A bug, a full disk or a single database server can still take the shop down — your design is only as available as its weakest single component. Availability also multiplies: if the web tier earns 99.99% but every request needs one database VM at 99.9%, the chain is roughly 0.9999 × 0.999 ≈ 99.89%, worse than either part. Fix the weakest link first.

Microsoft now recommends Virtual Machine Scale Sets with Flexible orchestration for new highly available designs: they spread VMs across zones or fault domains and add the scaling features you need for 12.12.

2. Virtual Machine Scale Sets: Flexible or Uniform

A Virtual Machine Scale Set manages a group of VMs from one model: image, size, network settings, extensions and cloud-init. It spreads instances across zones and fault domains, connects them to a load balancer or Application Gateway, adds and removes instances (manually or with autoscale), upgrades them and repairs them. Two decisions control what happens when it removes instances: the scale-in policy (Default balances zones and fault domains; NewestVM and OldestVM do what they say) and instance protection, which keeps chosen instances out of scale-in.

Every scale set has an orchestration mode, chosen at creation and fixed for its whole life.

| Flexible (recommended) | Uniform
Instances are | Standard VMs (Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines) | Scale-set VMs managed through scale-set APIs
Manage instances with | Normal VM commands, tags, RBAC, Azure Backup, Site Recovery | Scale-set VM commands only
Mix sizes, OS and pricing | Yes — even Spot and regular instances in one set | No — identical instances, all Spot or all regular
Scale | Up to 1,000 VMs | Large fleets of identical instances
Default outbound internet access | No — needs an explicit method | Yes
Health signal for repairs | Application Health extension | Application Health extension or load balancer probe
Automatic OS image upgrades | No (use guest patching instead) | Yes
Typical use | New workloads, including Nusantara's storefront | Existing fleets and platforms built on it

Since November 2023, the Azure CLI and PowerShell create Flexible scale sets unless you ask otherwise. For Nusantara Retail the choice is easy: Flexible instances are ordinary VMs, so everything learned in Lunch 06 still applies. A Flexible set can even adopt existing VMs, and instances that autoscale adds get a name made of a prefix you choose plus a unique suffix.

Spreading comes in two styles. With max spreading — the setting used with zones — Azure places instances across as many fault domains as it can. With fixed spreading, instances land in two or three fault domains you can see and even choose, which suits quorum-based software such as clustered databases that must know where each replica lives.

Warning: Instances in a Flexible scale set get no default outbound internet access. Without a NAT gateway on the subnet (the usual choice), load balancer outbound rules or a public IP per instance, package installs and OS updates fail and patch assessments can't reach the update sources — while the website itself keeps answering through the load balancer, so nobody notices until patch day.

3. Autoscale: rules, profiles and cool-downs

Autoscale is an Azure Monitor feature: an autoscale setting attached to the scale set (one per resource) decides when to add or remove instances. A setting holds up to 20 profiles. The default profile applies when no other profile matches; a recurrence profile repeats on chosen days, such as weekends; a fixed-date profile covers one event, such as 12.12. Each profile sets a minimum, a maximum and a default instance count, plus up to ten rules.

Part of a metric rule | Example | What it means
Metric | Percentage CPU of the scale set | A host metric, collected without any agent
Time grain and statistic | 1 minute, Average | One sample per minute, averaged across all instances
Duration and time aggregation | 5 minutes, Average | Look back five minutes, so one spike doesn't trigger anything
Operator and threshold | Greater than 70 | The condition that fires the rule
Action | Increase count by 3 | Or by a percentage, or set an exact count
Cool-down | 5 minutes | How long this rule waits after any scale action before it may act again

The autoscale engine runs every 30 to 60 seconds. If any scale-out rule fires, it scales out — to the largest count any rule asks for. It scales in only if all scale-in rules agree, and then by the smallest amount. The arithmetic for 12.12 is simple: three instances averaging 90% trigger the rule, three more arrive, and the same work spread over six instances averages about 45% — inside the quiet band, so nothing else happens until the crowd changes.

Before it scales in, autoscale checks whether the smaller set would immediately trip a scale-out rule. Suppose four instances average 60% and the scale-in rule says "below 65%". Removing one would put the same load on three instances — about 80% each, above the 70% scale-out threshold — so autoscale holds back rather than flap between three and four instances. Leave a wide gap instead: out above 70%, in below 30%. Two more details matter in production: if metrics can't be read and the set is below its default count, autoscale scales out to that default as a safety net; and every setting can email people or call a webhook when it scales, while the portal's Run history shows each decision.

Metric rules react; schedules anticipate. For 12.12, Nusantara adds a fixed-date profile from 22:00 on 11 December to 03:00 on 13 December with a minimum of six, so the first wave at midnight hits warm servers instead of waiting five minutes for the rule plus a few more for new VMs to boot. Metric rules still work inside that profile. Autoscale can also use other metrics — guest memory from an agent, the length of a Service Bus queue, requests from Application Insights — when CPU is not the real bottleneck.

Tip: Scale out early and generously; scale in slowly, one instance at a time. And test with real load: CPU rules on burstable B-series sizes can mislead you, because a VM that has spent its credits is throttled to its baseline and reports low CPU even while it struggles.

4. Identical instances, kept healthy

A scale set is only useful if every instance is the same. There are two ways to get there, and most teams mix them:

Approach | How it works | Strength | Weakness
Bake | Build a custom image with the app already installed | Fast, predictable boots | Every change means a new image
Fry | Start from a Marketplace image; configure on first boot with cloud-init or an extension | Easy to change | Slower boots; depends on download sources

For baking, an Azure Compute Gallery stores image definitions (OS, generation, security type) and numbered image versions, replicates them to the regions you choose and shares them across subscriptions — and it supports Trusted Launch, which older managed images do not. Azure VM Image Builder automates the bake: from a template it starts with a base image, runs your scripts and updates, and publishes a new version to the gallery. For frying, cloud-init reads custom data on first boot, and extensions — Custom Script, Application Health, Azure Monitor Agent and others — are part of the scale set model, so every new instance receives them.

When the model changes, the upgrade policy decides what happens to existing instances. Manual changes only new instances until you upgrade the others. Automatic updates every instance at once, which risks downtime. Rolling upgrades in batches — by default at most 20% of instances per batch — checks health between batches and can create extra instances first (max surge) so capacity never drops.

Automatic instance repairs watch a health signal, usually the Application Health extension calling an endpoint such as /health inside each instance: a 200 OK means healthy, anything else — including no answer — means unhealthy. When an instance stays unhealthy, the scale set replaces it with a fresh one built from the current model (the default), or reimages or restarts it. A grace period of 10 to 90 minutes after any change prevents repairs while an instance is still booting, protected instances are skipped, and repairs run in small batches — never more than 5% of the set at once, one at a time in sets under 20 — so a bad deployment can't wipe out everything together.

5. Cheaper, isolated and patched: Spot, hosts, placement and updates

Azure Spot Virtual Machines run on Azure's spare capacity at a deep discount, with no SLA. When Azure needs the capacity back — or when the price rises above a maximum you set — the VM is evicted, with a warning of up to 30 seconds through Scheduled Events. The eviction policy is Deallocate (disks remain and are billed; the VM can be restarted later) or Delete. A maximum price of -1 means "never evict me for price, and never charge more than the regular price". Spot has its own vCPU quota, doesn't support B-series sizes, and is available only on some subscription offers. When you create one, the portal shows each size's recent Spot prices and hourly eviction rate, and Azure Resource Graph exposes the same history, so you can pick sizes that are rarely evicted. A VM's priority is fixed at creation: you can't turn a regular VM into a Spot VM or back. Flexible scale sets can even mix a base of regular instances with Spot ones on top. Spot suits batch jobs, build agents and test environments — work that can stop and resume — never the checkout.

Spot is the cheapest capacity; sometimes you need the surest. On 12.12 every retailer in the region scales at midnight. An on-demand capacity reservation holds capacity for a VM size in a region or zone, and is billed like running VMs whether you use it or not. Don't confuse it with a reservation from Lunch 06, which is only a billing discount and guarantees no capacity at all.

Azure Dedicated Hosts give you a whole physical server, used only by your VMs, for strict isolation, control over maintenance timing or licensing that counts physical cores; you pay for the host. Proximity placement groups keep VMs physically close for the lowest possible latency between them, which works against spreading them out — so they are used with a single zone or none.

Azure Update Manager keeps the fleet patched without Azure Automation or Log Analytics. It assesses machines on demand or every 24 hours (periodic assessment), installs updates immediately, or follows maintenance configurations — schedules with a time window that can target machines dynamically, for example by tag or resource group. Each VM also has a patch orchestration mode: on Linux, ImageDefault leaves patching to the operating system's own settings, while AutomaticByPlatform lets Azure install critical and security updates itself in an availability-first rollout that never patches two availability zones at the same time (standalone VMs are patched during their off-peak hours). Hotpatching installs updates without a reboot on supported Windows Server editions. Update Manager is free for Azure VMs and charged per server for machines connected through Azure Arc, and it replaces the retired Automation Update Management. Like any patching tool, it needs outbound access to the update sources.

Trusted Launch protects the boot process with Secure Boot, a virtual TPM and boot integrity monitoring reported to Microsoft Defender for Cloud. It is the default for new Generation 2 VMs and scale sets created from the portal, CLI or PowerShell, at no extra cost.

Finally, Azure Virtual Desktop delivers Windows desktops and apps from VMs in Azure. Pools of multi-session Windows 11 Enterprise hosts can serve many users each and scale on a schedule — a candidate for the store managers' back-office applications, but a topic for another day.

6. Nusantara Retail's 12.12 design

Here is how the pieces answer Ibu Sari's two rules:

- Zones, not a single VM. A Flexible scale set spans zones 1, 2 and 3 in Indonesia Central, with at least three instances — one per zone — behind the Standard load balancer from Lunch 09.
- Autoscale. CPU above 70% for five minutes adds three instances; below 30% for five minutes removes one; a five-minute cool-down; maximum 12. A fixed-date profile keeps at least six instances through the 12.12 night.
- Headroom for a lost zone. If one zone of three fails at the peak, the other two must carry everything, so the maximum must leave room to grow — another reason the cap is 12, not 6.
- Identical and healthy. A weekly image from VM Image Builder in an Azure Compute Gallery, the Application Health extension on /health, automatic repairs, and rolling upgrades with max surge.
- Patched and secure. Trusted Launch on every instance, a NAT gateway for explicit outbound access, and an Update Manager maintenance configuration for Tuesdays at 02:00 WIB.
- Cheap where it's safe. Spot VMs process product-photo thumbnails overnight; checkout never runs on Spot.

Several later lunches build on this: Application Gateway and Front Door (Lunch 27) put a layer-7 front door before the scale set, Lunch 29's Kubernetes node pools are themselves scale sets, and Lunch 30 turns the scale set's metrics into dashboards and alerts.

Pause and think: at the 12.12 peak the storefront needs nine busy instances. Zone 2 fails at 00:40. With a maximum of 9, what happens to response times — and what minimum, maximum and zone layout would let two surviving zones carry the whole peak?

Field notes from Stefanus

Lose a zone on paper before you trust autoscale. Before I sign off on any autoscale setting, I do one sum out loud: take the busiest hour, write off every instance in one zone, and check that the instances the maximum still allows can carry the whole load below the scale-out threshold. If they can't, the cap is a budget decision dressed up as a capacity plan, and I want that written down. Next, I run a package update from inside one instance — not just a page request through the load balancer — because a fleet that serves customers but can't reach its update sources looks perfectly healthy until patch day. And I ask to see the scale-in, not just the scale-out: a set that grows on cue but never shrinks is the most expensive way to pass a load test.

Go further

- Microsoft Learn: Orchestration modes for Virtual Machine Scale Sets (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/virtual-machine-scale-sets/virtual-machine-scale-sets-orchestration-modes) — the full Flexible versus Uniform feature comparison.
- Microsoft Learn: Understand autoscale settings (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/azure-monitor/autoscale/autoscale-understanding-settings) — profiles, rule schema and how evaluation and cool-downs work.
- Microsoft Learn: Azure Spot Virtual Machines (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/virtual-machines/spot-vms) — eviction policies, pricing history and limitations.
- Microsoft Learn: What is Azure Update Manager? (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/update-manager/overview) — assessment, scheduled patching and hotpatching.

quiz.q: Pak Budi proposes putting the two storefront VMs in an availability set "because it's free and has a 99.95% SLA". Indonesia Central has three zones. What do you recommend, and why?
quiz.a: Spread the VMs across availability zones — ideally with a Flexible scale set — for 99.99% and protection against a whole-datacenter failure — why: an availability set only protects against rack and maintenance failures inside one datacenter.

quiz.q: Dewi wants to run a few Spot instances next to regular ones in the same scale set, tag individual instances and back up one of them with Azure Backup. Which orchestration mode does she need?
quiz.a: Flexible orchestration — why: its instances are standard VMs that support tags, RBAC and Azure Backup, and it can mix Spot and regular priority instances; a Uniform set's instances are all Spot or all regular.

quiz.q: An autoscale setting scales out when average CPU is above 70% and scales in when it is below 65%. Its run history shows that it rarely scales in, and when it does, it soon scales back out. What is wrong?
quiz.a: The thresholds are too close: removing one instance pushes the average straight back above 70%, so the flapping check blocks most scale-ins and the rest bounce back — why: autoscale needs a wide gap between thresholds (for example, scale in below 30%) plus a cool-down on each rule.

quiz.q: The finance team suggests running the checkout tier entirely on Spot VMs with a maximum price of -1 "so they never get evicted". What's the flaw?
quiz.a: A maximum price of -1 only prevents eviction for price; Spot VMs are still evicted whenever Azure needs the capacity, with about 30 seconds' notice and no SLA — why: Spot suits interruptible work like batch jobs, not the checkout.

quiz.q: A new Flexible scale set behind a public load balancer serves the website perfectly, but Update Manager's assessment fails and apt-get update times out on every instance. What is missing?
quiz.a: An explicit outbound method — a NAT gateway on the subnet, load balancer outbound rules, or instance public IPs — why: Flexible instances get no default outbound access, and inbound traffic through the load balancer does not give them a way out.

takeaways: Single VM, availability set and availability zones survive different failures; at the time of writing, 2+ VMs across zones earn 99.99% and 2+ VMs in an availability set 99.95%.
Flexible scale sets are the recommended default: standard VMs, mixed sizes and Spot, spread across zones — and they need explicit outbound access.
Autoscale = profiles (default, recurrence, fixed-date) + metric rules (metric, window, threshold, action, cool-down); scale out fast, scale in slowly, and keep a wide gap between thresholds.
Images from an Azure Compute Gallery, cloud-init and extensions keep instances identical; upgrade policies and automatic repairs keep them current and healthy.

Spot is for interruptible work; dedicated hosts and proximity placement groups solve niche isolation and latency needs; Update Manager and Trusted Launch keep the fleet patched and its boot chain protected.

lab.title: Ready for the 12.12 sale
lab.text:
What you'll build

Nusantara Retail's storefront outgrows its single VM. You build a Flexible scale set called vmss-web that spreads its instances across availability zones 1, 2 and 3, behind the Standard load balancer lb-nusa-web that setup.sh prepares. Every instance runs the course's small web server from cloud-init and reaches the internet only through a NAT gateway — explicit outbound access. Autoscale keeps two to three instances depending on CPU: you create your own 12.12 rush with a load script and watch Azure add an instance in the empty zone, then remove it after the cool-down. You finish by checking the instances for missing patches with Azure Update Manager, optionally watching a Spot VM get evicted, and repairing an outage that only shows up on patch day. The lab runs in $LOCATION (Southeast Asia by default); the production design in the reading uses Indonesia Central.

Before you start

- An Azure subscription where you can create resources (see Lab 01 (https://stefpin.github.io/azure-fundamentals-lunches/en/labs/01-before-you-begin.html)).
- Azure Cloud Shell (Bash) — open shell.azure.com. Nothing to install.
- Get the lab files, load the shared settings and set the scale-set sizes for this lab:

git clone https://github.com/stefpin/azure-fundamentals-lunches.git   # first time only
cd azure-fundamentals-lunches/labs/23-virtual-machines-advanced
source ../common/config.sh
RG=$(rg_name 23)
export INSTANCES=2 AS_MIN=2 AS_MAX=3
echo "Resource group: $RG · region: $LOCATION · size: $VM_SIZE_SMALL · image: $VM_IMAGE"

- Create the starting point — about 3 minutes:

bash setup.sh

setup.sh first checks that $VM_SIZE_SMALL is offered in all three zones of your region and that your vCPU quota covers the autoscale maximum. Then it creates the virtual network with a private subnet, the NAT gateway, the network security group nsg-web and the load balancer with its /health probe. The scale set itself is yours to build.

- Watch your vCPU quota. Each instance uses the default lab size Standard_B2ats_v2 (2 vCPUs). With the default settings the scale set runs 2 instances and at most 3 during the load test — up to 6 vCPUs. setup.sh checks your quota before it builds anything.

Warning: Small quota? Free trials often allow only 4 vCPUs per region. If setup.sh reports too little quota, use the small-quota settings below and run bash setup.sh again to re-check. The tasks work the same way; with one instance at the start, you see the second zone only after the scale-out. (Older sizes such as Standard_B1s are not an option: new subscriptions can't deploy B-series v1 any more.)

Setting | Default | Small-quota settings
VM_SIZE_SMALL | Standard_B2ats_v2 (2 vCPUs) | Standard_B2ats_v2 (2 vCPUs)
INSTANCES / AS_MIN / AS_MAX | 2 / 2 / 3 | 1 / 1 / 2
Most vCPUs at once | 6 | 4

export INSTANCES=1 AS_MIN=1 AS_MAX=2

Important: Lab resources cost money while they exist — the NAT gateway and both public IPs are billed by the hour even when no instance runs. Finish with the Clean up section, even if you stop halfway.

Tip: Cloud Shell disconnects after about 20 minutes without input and forgets your variables. If that happens, cd back into the lab folder and run the source, RG= and export lines again — and LB_IP= from Task 3.

Choose your mode

Mode | For you if… | How
Guided | you want every step explained | follow Tasks 1–7 below
Challenge | you already know the basics | read only the Challenge brief, build it your way, then run bash verify.sh

Task 1 · Look at the starting point

setup.sh built the network around the scale set so this lab can focus on the VMs. Take two minutes to see what the instances will plug into.

az resource list -g "$RG" --query "[].{type:type, name:name}" -o table

az network vnet subnet show -g "$RG" --vnet-name vnet-nusa-web -n snet-web \
  --query "{prefix:addressPrefix, natGateway:natGateway.id, defaultOutboundAccess:defaultOutboundAccess, subnetNsg:networkSecurityGroup.id}" \
  -o yaml

az network lb probe list -g "$RG" --lb-name lb-nusa-web \
  --query "[].{name:name, protocol:protocol, port:port, path:requestPath}" -o table

az network lb rule list -g "$RG" --lb-name lb-nusa-web \
  --query "[].{name:name, frontendPort:frontendPort, backendPort:backendPort, outboundSnatDisabled:disableOutboundSnat}" -o table

Three details matter later:

- The subnet is private (defaultOutboundAccess: false) and its explicit way out is the NAT gateway. Flexible scale-set instances never get default outbound access anyway, so without the NAT gateway they couldn't reach the Ubuntu mirrors.
- There is no NSG on the subnet (subnetNsg: null). The scale set will put nsg-web, which allows HTTP from the internet, on every instance's network interface. Standard load balancers are closed to inbound traffic until an NSG allows it.
- The load-balancing rule has outbound SNAT disabled: the load balancer handles inbound traffic only. Its probe asks each instance for /health on port 80 — the shared cloud-init web server answers ok there.

Checkpoint: the resource list shows six resources: two public IP addresses (pip-lb-web, pip-ng-web), the NAT gateway ng-nusa-web, the virtual network, the network security group and the load balancer. The probe table shows probe-health on HTTP port 80 with path /health.

Task 2 · Create a Flexible scale set across three zones

One command creates the scale set, its instances, their disks and network interfaces, and adds the instances to the load balancer's backend pool. It takes three to five minutes.

az vmss create \
  --resource-group "$RG" \
  --name vmss-web \
  --location "$LOCATION" \
  --orchestration-mode Flexible \
  --image "$VM_IMAGE" \
  --vm-sku "$VM_SIZE_SMALL" \
  --instance-count "$INSTANCES" \
  --zones 1 2 3 \
  --platform-fault-domain-count 1 \
  --vnet-name vnet-nusa-web \
  --subnet snet-web \
  --nsg nsg-web \
  --lb lb-nusa-web \
  --backend-pool-name bep-web \
  --custom-data "$AZL_COMMON_DIR/cloud-init-web.yml" \
  --admin-username "$ADMIN_USER" \
  --generate-ssh-keys \
  --storage-sku StandardSSD_LRS \
  --upgrade-policy-mode Manual \
  --output none

Option | Why
--orchestration-mode Flexible | Every instance is an ordinary VM. Flexible is already the CLI default; writing it out documents the choice, which can't be changed later
--zones 1 2 3 | Instances are spread across three datacenters; Azure tries to keep the zones balanced as the set grows and shrinks
--platform-fault-domain-count 1 | Max spreading: inside each zone, Azure spreads instances over as many fault domains as it can — the recommended setting with zones
--vm-sku "$VM_SIZE_SMALL" | The size of every instance in the model (Standard_B2ats_v2 by default)
--nsg nsg-web | The existing NSG goes on each instance's network interface, so HTTP from the internet is allowed
--lb lb-nusa-web --backend-pool-name bep-web | New instances — including those autoscale adds later — join the backend pool automatically
--custom-data …/cloud-init-web.yml | cloud-init starts a small web server on port 80 that shows the host name and zone, plus /health
--upgrade-policy-mode Manual | Model changes reach existing instances only when you upgrade them; new instances always use the latest model

There is no public IP and no SSH rule: you will run commands inside the instances with Run Command instead. Now look at the scale set and its instances:

az vmss show -g "$RG" -n vmss-web \
  --query "{mode:orchestrationMode, zones:join(',', zones), faultDomains:platformFaultDomainCount, size:sku.name, capacity:sku.capacity}" -o table

az vm list -g "$RG" -d \
  --query "[?virtualMachineScaleSet].{name:name, zone:zones[0], size:hardwareProfile.vmSize, power:powerState, privateIp:privateIps}" -o table

Because Flexible instances are ordinary VMs, az vm list shows them, and every az vm command you learned in Lab 06 works on them.

Tip: Prefer the portal? Home › Virtual Machine Scale Sets › Create. On Basics: your resource group, name vmss-web, your region, availability zones 1, 2, 3, orchestration mode Flexible, security type Trusted launch virtual machines, scaling mode Manual with instance count 2, image Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS – x64 Gen2, your size, username azureuser and Use existing public key (paste cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub). On Networking: virtual network vnet-nusa-web; edit the network interface to use subnet snet-web, the advanced NSG option with nsg-web and no public IP; under Load balancing choose Azure load balancer, lb-nusa-web and backend pool bep-web. On Advanced: paste the contents of labs/common/cloud-init-web.yml into Custom data. Then Review + create.

Checkpoint: the scale set shows mode Flexible, zones 1,2,3 and fault domains 1. The VM list shows $INSTANCES instances whose names start with vmss-web_, each VM running, in different zones.

Task 3 · Test through the load balancer

Shoppers only ever see the load balancer's address. Ask it for the page several times:

LB_IP=$(az network public-ip show -g "$RG" -n pip-lb-web --query ipAddress -o tsv)
echo "http://$LB_IP/"
for i in {1..8}; do
  curl -s -m 5 "http://$LB_IP/" | grep -o 'Served by.*' | sed -e 's/<[^>]*>//g'
done
curl -s "http://$LB_IP/health"

Each curl opens a new connection, and the load balancer spreads connections across the healthy instances, so the answers alternate between host names — and zones. The last line prints ok, the answer the health probe receives every few seconds. Open the address in your browser, too.

If nothing prints yet, wait a minute: cloud-init is still starting the web server, and the load balancer sends no traffic to an instance until its /health probe succeeds.

Checkpoint: you see lines such as Served by <host name> in availability zone 1. from two different hosts in two different zones (one host with the small-quota settings), and /health returns ok.

Task 4 · Add autoscale rules

Autoscale is an Azure Monitor setting attached to the scale set. Create it with the instance limits, then add one rule to scale out and one to scale in:

az monitor autoscale create \
  --resource-group "$RG" \
  --resource vmss-web \
  --resource-type Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachineScaleSets \
  --name autoscale-web \
  --min-count "$AS_MIN" --max-count "$AS_MAX" --count "$AS_MIN" \
  --output none

az monitor autoscale rule create -g "$RG" --autoscale-name autoscale-web \
  --condition "Percentage CPU > 70 avg 5m" --scale out 1 --cooldown 5 --output none

az monitor autoscale rule create -g "$RG" --autoscale-name autoscale-web \
  --condition "Percentage CPU < 30 avg 5m" --scale in 1 --cooldown 5 --output none

Read the first rule the way the engine does: when the average Percentage CPU across the scale set over the last five minutes is above 70%, add one instance, then wait five minutes before this rule may act again. The wide gap between 70% and 30% stops the set from flapping, and the maximum of three keeps you inside a small vCPU quota. Check what you built:

az monitor autoscale show -g "$RG" -n autoscale-web \
  --query "{enabled:enabled, minimum:profiles[0].capacity.minimum, maximum:profiles[0].capacity.maximum, default:profiles[0].capacity.default}" -o table

az monitor autoscale rule list -g "$RG" --autoscale-name autoscale-web \
  --query "[].{metric:metricTrigger.metricName, operator:metricTrigger.operator, threshold:metricTrigger.threshold, window:metricTrigger.timeWindow, direction:scaleAction.direction, change:scaleAction.value, cooldown:scaleAction.cooldown}" -o table

Tip: Prefer the portal? vmss-web › Scaling › Custom autoscale. Choose Scale based on a metric, set the instance limits (minimum 2, maximum 3, default 2), then Add a rule: Percentage CPU, greater than 70, duration 5 minutes, Increase count by 1, cool down 5 minutes. Add a second rule: less than 30, Decrease count by 1. Save. The portal names the setting for you; verify.sh finds it through the scale set.

Checkpoint: autoscale is enabled with minimum $AS_MIN and maximum $AS_MAX, and the rule table shows two Percentage CPU rules — GreaterThan 70 with direction Increase, and LessThan 30 with direction Decrease — each changing the count by 1, with a five-minute window and cool-down (PT5M).

Task 5 · Create a 12.12 rush and watch autoscale

Real shoppers are hard to summon at lunchtime, so fake the rush: load-cpu.sh keeps every vCPU of an instance busy for 15 minutes and then stops by itself. Run Command copies it into each instance and runs it there:

for vm in $(az vm list -g "$RG" --query "[?virtualMachineScaleSet].name" -o tsv); do
  az vm run-command invoke -g "$RG" -n "$vm" --command-id RunShellScript \
    --scripts @load-cpu.sh --parameters 900 --query "value[0].message" -o tsv
done

Each instance answers CPU load started on … for 900 seconds. Now watch the average CPU and the instance count once a minute (press Ctrl+C to stop watching):

VMSS_ID=$(az vmss show -g "$RG" -n vmss-web --query id -o tsv)
while true; do
  cpu=$(az monitor metrics list --resource "$VMSS_ID" --metric "Percentage CPU" --interval PT1M \
        --aggregation Average --offset 1h \
        --query "value[0].timeseries[0].data[?average] | [-1].average" -o tsv)
  count=$(az vm list -g "$RG" --query "length([?virtualMachineScaleSet])" -o tsv)
  printf '%s  average CPU: %5.1f%%  instances: %s\n' "$(date +%H:%M)" "${cpu:-0}" "$count"
  sleep 60
done

What to expect (timings vary by a few minutes):

Minutes after the load starts | What happens
0–3 | CPU climbs to about 100% on every instance; the metric lags one to three minutes behind
about 6–10 | The five-minute average passes 70%, so autoscale adds one instance. The count goes up while the new VM is still being created
about 10–13 | The new instance runs — usually in the zone that had none — and gets traffic from the load balancer once /health answers
15 | The load stops by itself
about 20–25 | The five-minute average is below 30% and the cool-down is over, so autoscale removes one instance

Notice that the average drops when the new instance arrives — to about 67% with the default settings, about 50% with the small-quota settings — because the new instance has no load of its own. In a real shop the load balancer would send it shoppers, and every instance would cool down. Run the curl loop from Task 3 again to see the new host name.

Autoscale records every decision. Ask the activity log, or open vmss-web › Scaling › Run history in the portal:

az monitor activity-log list -g "$RG" --offset 1h \
  --query "[?category.value=='Autoscale'].{time:eventTimestamp, operation:operationName.localizedValue, status:status.localizedValue}" -o table

While you wait for the scale-in, do Task 6. Want it sooner? Stop the load now — scale-in follows about ten minutes later:

for vm in $(az vm list -g "$RG" --query "[?virtualMachineScaleSet].name" -o tsv); do
  az vm run-command invoke -g "$RG" -n "$vm" --command-id RunShellScript \
    --scripts @load-cpu.sh --parameters stop --query "value[0].message" -o tsv
done

Note: Burstable credits. B-series instances earn CPU credits while they idle and spend them when they run above their baseline. A brand-new instance starts with only a small balance, so if you repeat the load test several times the instances run out of credits: CPU is then capped at the baseline, and autoscale may see modest CPU while the instances struggle — the trap from the reading. The CPU Credits Remaining metric shows how much is left.

Checkpoint: the watch loop showed the instance count go from $AS_MIN to $AS_MAX, and later back to $AS_MIN. The activity log (or Run history) lists a scale-up and a scale-down.

Task 6 · Assess patches with Azure Update Manager

Patching a fleet by hand doesn't scale, and an instance that autoscale added last night is as exposed as the first one. Azure Update Manager checks machines for missing updates on demand or every 24 hours (periodic assessment), and installs them now or in a maintenance window. Assess the first instance — it takes two to five minutes:

FIRST_VM=$(az vm list -g "$RG" --query "[?virtualMachineScaleSet].name | [0]" -o tsv)
az vm assess-patches -g "$RG" -n "$FIRST_VM" \
  --query "{status:status, criticalAndSecurity:criticalAndSecurityPatchCount, other:otherPatchCount, rebootPending:rebootPending, examples:availablePatches[:5].name}" \
  -o yaml

The assessment runs inside the instance: it refreshes the package lists from the Ubuntu mirrors — through the NAT gateway — and compares them with what is installed. How many updates you see depends on how old the Marketplace image is; zero is a perfectly good answer.

Tip: Prefer the portal? Azure Update Manager › Machines, filter on your resource group, select an instance and Check for updates. When it finishes, the Updates column shows the counts and the instance page lists each update. Open Schedule updates to see how a maintenance configuration (for example Tuesdays 02:00 WIB) would patch the whole fleet — then close it without saving.

Checkpoint: the status is Succeeded (or CompletedWithWarnings), and you can name the number of critical and security updates the instance is missing.

Task 7 · (Optional) A Spot VM and a simulated eviction

Spot VMs are cheap because Azure can take them back. Do this task after the scale set is back to $AS_MIN instances, so you stay at 4 vCPUs or fewer. Spot doesn't support B-series sizes, uses its own vCPU quota and isn't offered on every subscription type (free trial and student subscriptions may not have it). Check your Spot quota first:

az vm list-usage -l "$LOCATION" \
  --query "[?contains(localName, 'Low-priority') || contains(localName, 'Spot')].{quota:localName, used:currentValue, limit:limit}" -o table

If the limit is at least 2, create a Spot VM in the same subnet, without a public IP:

SPOT_SIZE=${SPOT_SIZE:-Standard_D2as_v5}
az vm create \
  --resource-group "$RG" --name vm-spot-1 --location "$LOCATION" \
  --image "$VM_IMAGE" --size "$SPOT_SIZE" \
  --priority Spot --eviction-policy Deallocate --max-price -1 \
  --vnet-name vnet-nusa-web --subnet snet-web --nsg "" --public-ip-address "" \
  --os-disk-delete-option Delete --nic-delete-option Delete \
  --admin-username "$ADMIN_USER" --generate-ssh-keys --storage-sku StandardSSD_LRS --output table

az vm show -g "$RG" -n vm-spot-1 \
  --query "{priority:priority, evictionPolicy:evictionPolicy, maxPrice:billingProfile.maxPrice}" -o table

--max-price -1 means "never evict me because of the price, and never charge more than the regular price". --eviction-policy Deallocate keeps the disk when the VM is evicted. Now play Azure and take the capacity back:

az vm simulate-eviction -g "$RG" -n vm-spot-1
for i in {1..40}; do
  state=$(az vm get-instance-view -g "$RG" -n vm-spot-1 \
    --query "instanceView.statuses[?starts_with(code, 'PowerState/')].displayStatus | [0]" -o tsv)
  echo "$(date +%H:%M:%S)  $state"
  [[ "$state" == "VM deallocated" ]] && break
  sleep 15
done

A deallocated Spot VM costs nothing for compute, but its disk is still billed and its vCPUs still count against your Spot quota. Delete it:

az vm delete -g "$RG" -n vm-spot-1 --yes

Checkpoint: the power state went from VM running to VM deallocated without you stopping anything, and vm-spot-1 is gone from az vm list -g "$RG" -o table. If the VM couldn't be created because of quota or your subscription type, skip this task — verify.sh doesn't check it.

Break it and fix it

Head office's network team spots the NAT gateway on the bill and removes it from the subnet "because the website still works without it". Play the network team:

az network vnet subnet update -g "$RG" --vnet-name vnet-nusa-web -n snet-web --remove natGateway --output none
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' "http://$LB_IP/"
FIRST_VM=$(az vm list -g "$RG" --query "[?virtualMachineScaleSet].name | [0]" -o tsv)
az vm run-command invoke -g "$RG" -n "$FIRST_VM" --command-id RunShellScript \
  --scripts "curl -sS -m 8 -o /dev/null -w 'HTTP %{http_code}\n' http://archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu/ || echo 'No outbound internet access'" \
  --query "value[0].message" -o tsv

Symptom: the shop still answers 200 — but the instance can't reach the Ubuntu mirrors any more (Connection timed out, then No outbound internet access). Nobody notices until patch day: apt fails, patch assessments can't refresh their package lists, and bash verify.sh fails one check. Explain why the website still works, then fix it without looking at the hint.

Hint and fix

Shoppers' connections start on the internet, arrive through the load balancer and are answered through it, so inbound traffic is unaffected. Connections that the instances start need an explicit outbound method: Flexible scale-set instances have no default outbound access, the subnet is private, and the load-balancing rule has outbound SNAT disabled — the NAT gateway was the only way out. Attach it again:

az network vnet subnet update -g "$RG" --vnet-name vnet-nusa-web -n snet-web --nat-gateway ng-nusa-web --output none
az vm run-command invoke -g "$RG" -n "$FIRST_VM" --command-id RunShellScript \
  --scripts "curl -sS -m 8 -o /dev/null -w 'HTTP %{http_code}\n' http://archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu/ || echo 'No outbound internet access'" \
  --query "value[0].message" -o tsv

The second command prints HTTP 200 again. Load balancer outbound rules would also work, but a NAT gateway is the method Microsoft recommends, and it scales to many instances without running out of ports.

Verify your work

bash verify.sh

Every check should say PASS. If one fails, the message tells you which task to revisit. If you used the small-quota settings (at most 4 vCPUs), make sure AS_MIN and AS_MAX are still exported in your shell (echo $AS_MIN $AS_MAX) so the script expects your limits.

Clean up (do not skip!)

bash cleanup.sh

This deletes everything the lab created: the resource group rg-lunch23-<suffix> with the scale set, its VMs, disks and network interfaces, the autoscale setting, the load balancer, the NAT gateway, both public IPs and the optional Spot VM. Nothing lives outside the resource group. Deletion continues in the background for a few minutes.

Troubleshooting

Symptom | Likely cause | Fix
SkuNotAvailable … "The requested size for resource … is currently not available in location … zones …" | The size isn't offered to your subscription in that region or in every zone (B-series v1 sizes such as Standard_B1s are closed to new subscriptions) | Pick another current 2-vCPU size (export VM_SIZE_SMALL=Standard_B2ts_v2, then bash setup.sh to re-check), delete the failed set (az vmss delete -g "$RG" -n vmss-web) and run Task 2 again
"Operation could not be completed as it results in exceeding approved Total Regional Cores quota" (or a VM family quota) | Other VMs use your vCPUs, or the quota is smaller than 6 | Delete leftovers from other labs (bash ../common/check-environment.sh lists them), use the small-quota settings, or request more quota
curl to the load balancer prints nothing or 000 | cloud-init is still starting the web server, or the instances aren't in the backend pool | Wait two minutes; check az network lb address-pool show -g "$RG" --lb-name lb-nusa-web -n bep-web --query "length(loadBalancerBackendAddresses)"
Every answer comes from the same host | Only one instance passes the /health probe, or you use the small-quota settings with one instance | Check az vm list -g "$RG" -d -o table; wait for the new instance's web server to start
No scale-out after 15 minutes | The load didn't start, the average stayed below 70%, or the instances ran out of CPU credits | Check the Run Command messages and the watch loop; look at CPU Credits Remaining; repeat Task 5 after the credits recover
The set stays at 3 instances long after the test | Scale-in needs five minutes below 30% plus the cool-down, or the load is still running | Run the stop loop from Task 5 and wait ten minutes
Run Command fails with Conflict or "Run command extension execution is in progress" | Another Run Command (or a patch assessment) is still running on that instance | Wait a minute and run it again
az vm assess-patches returns Failed or an error | The instance can't reach the Ubuntu mirrors (NAT gateway missing), or its VM agent isn't ready yet | Re-attach the NAT gateway (Break it and fix it); wait a few minutes after creation and try again
Spot VM: "exceeding approved LowPriorityCores quota" or "not supported for this subscription offer" | Your Spot quota is too small, or your subscription type doesn't offer Spot | Skip Task 7, or request Spot quota on a pay-as-you-go subscription
Spot VM: SkuNotAvailable for Standard_D2as_v5 | No Spot capacity for that size right now | Try another 2-vCPU size: SPOT_SIZE=Standard_D2s_v5 and run the command again
setup.sh prints a note about --default-outbound | Your Azure CLI is older than the subnet setting | Nothing to do: Flexible scale-set instances have no default outbound access anyway
verify.sh fails on the minimum or maximum after using the small-quota settings | AS_MIN/AS_MAX weren't exported in the shell that runs verify.sh | export AS_MIN=1 AS_MAX=2, then bash verify.sh

Stretch goals

- Get ready for midnight. Add a fixed-date profile that keeps three instances through the 12.12 night (look up time zone names with az monitor autoscale profile list-timezones -q "SE Asia" -o table): az monitor autoscale profile create -g "$RG" --autoscale-name autoscale-web -n sale-1212 --copy-rules default --min-count 3 --count 3 --max-count 3 --start "2026-12-11 22:00:00" --end "2026-12-13 03:00:00" --timezone "SE Asia Standard Time". verify.sh checks only the default profile, so this doesn't change its result.
- Get told when it scales. az monitor autoscale update -g "$RG" -n autoscale-web --add-action email you@example.com (use your own address), then repeat Task 5.
- Watch the probe at work. Stop the web server on one instance (az vm run-command invoke -g "$RG" -n "$FIRST_VM" --command-id RunShellScript --scripts "systemctl stop nusa-web"), run the curl loop from Task 3 — every answer now comes from the other instances — then start it again with systemctl start nusa-web. With the Application Health extension and automatic repairs (reading, section 4), the scale set would replace such an instance by itself.
- Choose Spot sizes with data. Query recent eviction rates with Azure Resource Graph (the CLI may offer to install the resource-graph extension): az graph query -q "SpotResources | where type =~ 'microsoft.compute/skuspotevictionrate/location' | where location =~ '$LOCATION' | where sku.name in~ ('standard_d2as_v5', 'standard_d2s_v5') | project skuName=tostring(sku.name), evictionRate=tostring(properties.evictionRate)" -o table.

Challenge brief

Build the following, any way you like (portal, CLI, Bicep). You may run bash setup.sh for the network and load balancer, or build your own:

1. A resource group named rg-lunch23-<suffix> (rg_name 23) tagged course=azure-fundamentals-lunches and lunch=23 — setup.sh (or ensure_rg "$RG" 23) does this for you.
2. A Virtual Machine Scale Set named vmss-web with Flexible orchestration, spanning availability zones 1, 2 and 3, using size $VM_SIZE_SMALL and the shared web server labs/common/cloud-init-web.yml, with at least 2 running instances (1 with the small-quota settings).
3. Its instances in the backend pool of a Standard public load balancer with an HTTP health probe on /health and a rule for port 80, so that http://<load balancer IP>/ returns HTTP 200 and the Nusantara Retail page.
4. Explicit outbound internet access for the instances: a NAT gateway on their subnet (or load balancer outbound rules).
5. An enabled autoscale setting on the scale set whose default profile has minimum 2 and maximum 3 instances (1 and 2 with the small-quota settings), at least one Percentage CPU scale-out rule and at least one Percentage CPU scale-in rule.
6. Not checked by the script, but do it: generate CPU load and watch a scale-out and a scale-in, run a patch assessment, and (if your subscription allows Spot) create, evict and delete a Spot VM.

Then run bash verify.sh. Stuck? Peek at solution.sh or switch to Guided mode.
